coverage_summary: All 40 model-visible files were within scope; no files were excluded by the binary/sensitive filters. I read the complete source of every Java class in the snapshot (SlingServletResolver, ResolutionCache, the four helper/collector classes, PathBasedServletAcceptor, ScriptResource/ScriptResourceResolver/ScriptResourceDecorator/SlingScriptResolverImpl, the resource package, the bundle package, the defaults package, WebConsolePlugin, the JMX MBean/package-info) and the POM/findbugs/README/config files. The P1 relation scope reports 33 parsed Java files, 511 symbols, 767 syntax-level edges, 2158 call sites with 1887 unresolved calls and no semantic resolution/control-flow/data-flow; its only non-config facts were name-based output hints in DefaultErrorHandlerServlet, which I verified against source and found fully escaped. I traced the main inputs an HTTP client can influence (request path/selectors/extension/suffix/method, and the console `url`/`method` parameters) through resolution, path gating and output.
limitations: No code, tests, build or scanners were executed; all conclusions are static source reading only, and no finding was runtime-confirmed.

External dependencies are not in the snapshot: semantics of Sling API helpers (ResourceUtil.normalize/resourceTypeToPath/getXmlEscapingWriter/escapeXml), SlingUriBuilder, ResourceResolver.getResource normalization for '.'/'..' segments, JSON generator escaping and the scripting SPI (BundledRenderUnitFinder eval) could not be inspected and are assumed to behave as documented.

The P1 index does not implement control flow, data flow or semantic resolution (1887 unresolved calls), so call/reachability edges are navigation hints only and were verified individually against source text.

No tests or integration test resources exist in the snapshot, so intended behavior for edge cases (strict path servlets reached via resource-type search, execution-path defaults, resource-type traversal) could not be pinned down and was left as unconfirmed leads rather than findings.
Deployment-context actors (who may install bundles, write content, or access the Web Console) are not defined in the source; attacker-control assessments therefore rely on stated prerequisites.

rejected_leads.lead: Reflected XSS in WebConsolePlugin HTML output
rejected_leads.reason: Checked every HTML/JSON emission in console/WebConsolePlugin.java: the `url` parameter (line 288), `method` (166), resourcePath (162, 317), selectors (325), extension (331), suffix (337), servlet class/script/bundled names (424-435) all pass through ResponseUtil.escapeXml or StringEscapeUtils.escapeJson before printing. Only bundle.getSymbolicName()/bundleId (line 444) are emitted without escaping, but symbolic-name content originates from installed bundle metadata (privileged deployment), not from an HTTP request, so attacker control is not established in source.

rejected_leads.lead: XSS/HTML injection in DefaultErrorHandlerServlet (status message, request URI, stack trace, progress tracker)
rejected_leads.reason: renderHtml routes the exception stack trace and RequestProgressTracker dump through ResponseUtil.getXmlEscapingWriter, and sendIntro/sendEpilogue escape statusMessage, requestUri, servletName and serverInfo with ResponseUtil.escapeXml (lines 96-130, 230-299). renderJson uses a JSON generator that escapes values. No unescaped attacker-influenced output sink was found in this file.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal via resource type / resource super type in LocationCollector.handleResourceType (paths built as searchPath + ResourceUtil.resourceTypeToPath(resourceType) without ResourceUtil.normalize)
rejected_leads.reason: LocationCollector.java lines 135-151 and 195-218 compose paths from resource-type strings without normalization, but every resulting servlet/script candidate is re-checked with SlingServletResolver.isPathAllowed in ResourceCollector (lines 234, 369) and NamedScriptResourceCollector (97, 119), and the absolute-resource-type branch of SlingServletResolver (lines 457-479) normalizes and gates the path before adaptation. Attacker control of resource type requires content-write privileges, and the in-repo source cannot establish that a crafted type escapes the underlying resolver's own path handling, so impact is unproven.

rejected_leads.lead: PathBasedServletAcceptor (sling.servlet.paths.strict) not consulted for candidates found by the deep resource-type search
rejected_leads.reason: The strict extension/selector/method check is only invoked in the absolute-resource-type branch of resolveServletInternal (SlingServletResolver.java lines 462-467); the deep search via ResourceCollector.addLocationServlet (ResourceCollector.java 365-377) can select a path-mounted servlet without that check. Whether this deviates from intended upstream behavior could not be verified from source alone, and selection still requires the servlet to be mounted under a location derived from the request resource type, so this remains an unconfirmed hardening question, not an evidenced vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: ResourceCollector.getWeightedResources passes isDefaultExtension as the children-list caching flag to getChildrenList (ResourceCollector.java line 231)
rejected_leads.reason: The second parameter of AbstractResourceCollector.getChildrenList is `useCaching`; passing the default-extension boolean looks inconsistent, but it only affects whether per-Resolver child lists are cached (a correctness/performance concern). No security impact or cross-request data exposure was established, and the cache lives on the per-request/per-resolver property map.

summary: Reviewed the full visible snapshot of org.apache.sling.servlets.resolver (version 2.10.0, 40 files: 33 Java sources plus POM/manifest/docs). Coverage included the servlet/script resolution pipeline (SlingServletResolver, ResolutionCache, ResourceCollector, NamedScriptResourceCollector, LocationCollector, AbstractResourceCollector, WeightedResource), the path/execution-path gating (isPathAllowed/getExecutionPaths, PathBasedServletAcceptor), the ServletResourceProvider layer (ServletMounter, ServletResourceProviderFactory, MergingServletResourceProvider, ServletResource, SlingServletConfig), the bundled-script support (BundledScriptTracker, BundledScriptServlet, BundledRenderUnitCapabilityImpl, TypeProviderImpl, RequestWrapper, BundledHooks), ScriptResource/ScriptResourceResolver/ScriptResourceDecorator, the error handling path (DefaultErrorHandlerServlet, DefaultServlet, HandleError* wrappers) and the Web Console plugin. I traced attacker-controllable HTTP inputs (path, selectors, extension, suffix, method, `url`/`method` console parameters) into validation, resource lookups and output sinks. No candidate reached the required evidence threshold: each plausible lead failed either attacker-control, verified sanitization, or concrete impact when checked against the actual source text. I therefore submit no candidate rather than a speculative finding.
